<<The Airline Above the Shifting Map>>

Section 1  
When the pound fell after the vote, Mara Vale watched the figures slide across the glass wall of the airline’s headquarters like rain on a runway. Profits had dropped, fuel prices had offered less help than hoped, and every route into Europe now seemed to carry a second passenger: uncertainty.

Yet the planes were full. More travelers than ever were boarding, dragging bright suitcases through dawn-lit terminals, chasing holidays, work, family, and second chances. Mara, newly appointed to lead the airline, told her team that survival would not come from panic. It would come from sharper service, stronger airports, and the dare to keep flying when rivals were folding.

Section 2  
The company’s offices stood in a narrow tower beside the airport, where executives could see aircraft lifting through the grey morning. In one meeting, a lawyer explained the new ownership rules that might be needed after 2019. To keep flying freely across Europe, the airline would have to prove it was mainly owned and controlled by EU nationals.

Some British shareholders might one day be asked to sell. It sounded harsh, but Mara called it a technical step, not a betrayal. “We are not leaving our passengers behind,” she said. “We are building a bridge before the old one breaks.”

That evening, she visited her father, a retired mechanic who spent his Sundays fishing by the estuary. He told her that every storm changed the water, but not the skill of the person holding the line.

Section 3  
By spring, forward bookings were rising. Empty space left by failed competitors gave the airline fresh room to grow. Investors returned with cautious smiles, and newspapers wrote that the business had found opportunity in disruption.

At the annual gathering, Mara spoke not only of fares, costs, and routes, but of society itself: how people needed movement, how families stretched across borders, how cities depended on wings.

After the speech, a young cabin crew member handed her a small paper plane folded from the event program. On one wing, someone had written: “A difficult year is still a year survived.”

Mara laughed and kept it on her desk as a treat, a reminder that even in turbulent skies, a company could choose direction, lift, and nerve.
